title: Zane's Trace ends at Maysville
summary: In May 1796, Congress backed Col. Ebenezer Zane's plan to cut a road through the Northwest Territory "to speed up travel times to Kentucky." Built in 1796–97 with his brother…
bodyMarkdown:
In May 1796, Congress backed Col. Ebenezer Zane’s plan to cut a road through the Northwest Territory “to speed up travel times to Kentucky.” Zane had served in the Revolution, owned land at Wheeling, and stood to profit from tracts he would buy where the road crossed major rivers. The national interest still lined up with his petition. Built in 1796–97 with his brother Jonathan Zane, his son-in-law John McIntire, and a Native guide named Tomepomehala, the road ran more than 230 miles from Wheeling, Virginia (now West Virginia), to the Ohio River across from Maysville, then known as Limestone.

Much of the Trace followed older Native paths, including the Mingo Trail between present-day Fairview and Zanesville and the Moxahala Trail between Zanesville and Chillicothe. Chillicothe was the only settlement already on the route. The country was heavily forested and hilly; the first road was not easy for wagons. After Ohio became a state in 1803, a state transportation tax paid to clear stumps and widen the thoroughfare in 1804.

Rivers were crossed by ford or ferry. Zane ran a ferry at Wheeling; a bridge there waited until 1837. Other ferrymen worked Wills Creek at Cambridge, the Muskingum at Zanesville, the Hocking near Lancaster, and the Scioto at Chillicothe. Ferries also ran across the Ohio to Maysville. Aberdeen, Ohio, was founded on the north bank in 1816; a bridge between Aberdeen and Maysville was not built until 1931.

As part of his contract, Congress let Zane buy select tracts at the Muskingum, Hocking, and Scioto crossings. He deeded the Muskingum tract to Jonathan Zane and John McIntire; McIntire’s town of Westbourne became Zanesville in 1801. On the Hocking he laid out what became Lancaster. The Scioto tract, opposite already-settled Chillicothe and against Virginia military lands, was less useful and was sold on in 1804.

For settlers who did not want to float the Ohio all the way from Pittsburgh, Zane’s Trace made Maysville the overland door into the Bluegrass. Pack trains and later wagons came down to the river, crossed by ferry, and took the road south toward Lexington. That traffic helps explain why the Maysville–Lexington road mattered so much in the early commonwealth—and why Andrew Jackson’s 1830 veto of the Maysville Road bill became a national fight over internal improvements. Between 1825 and 1830 the segment of the Trace from Wheeling to Zanesville was rebuilt as part of the National Road.

## Kentucky today

Maysville still sits at the Kentucky end of the old Trace. The overland door Zane opened fed the Bluegrass for a generation before steamboats and the National Road rearranged the map. Clement Martzloff’s map of the Trace, held on Wikimedia Commons, remains the clearest single picture of the route from Wheeling to the Ohio opposite Maysville. See also [the Maysville Road and Jackson’s veto](/stories/the-maysville-road-and-jacksons-veto-1830/).
